question_text: A 28-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 0, at 32 weeks' gestation is evaluated for vaginal bleeding. Five days ago, she was admitted to the hospital and started on treatment for a deep vein thrombosis in the right leg. Her pulse is 125/min and blood pressure is 95/67 mm Hg. Physical examination shows large hematomas on the upper limbs and swelling in the right calf. There is a large amount of bright red blood in the vaginal vault. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin of 8.9 mg/dL, platelet count of 185,000/mm3, and activated partial thromboplastin time of 160 seconds. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy to rapidly reverse this patient's coagulopathy?

                    ### Question
                    A 28-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 0, at 32 weeks' gestation is evaluated for vaginal bleeding. Five days ago, she was admitted to the hospital and started on treatment for a deep vein thrombosis in the right leg. Her pulse is 125/min and blood pressure is 95/67 mm Hg. Physical examination shows large hematomas on the upper limbs and swelling in the right calf. There is a large amount of bright red blood in the vaginal vault. Laboratory studies show a hemoglobin of 8.9 mg/dL, platelet count of 185,000/mm3, and activated partial thromboplastin time of 160 seconds. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy to rapidly reverse this patient's coagulopathy?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Protamine sulfate
opb. Prothrombin complex concentrate
opc. Vitamin K
opd. Alteplase
ope. Fresh frozen plasma

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
In a case of severe bleeding due to anticoagulant therapy in a pregnant woman, Prothrombin Complex Concentrate (PCC) is the most appropriate choice for rapid reversal of coagulopathy. PCC acts quickly to replenish essential clotting factors, directly addressing the elevated aPTT and urgent clinical needs. Fresh Frozen Plasma, while effective, is slower and less suitable for immediate reversal. Vitamin K, although crucial for synthesis of clotting factors, acts too slowly to address acute bleeding. Protamine sulfate and Alteplase are not suitable for reversing the effects of vitamin K antagonists and could exacerbate bleeding, respectively.
